newsitem.title: USA: Feds detain ex-chief of NYSE top performer in '96.
newsitem.headline: Feds detain ex-chief of NYSE top performer in '96.

text.p: The former chief executive officer of the top performing New York Stock Exchange company in 1996 was ordered held without bail Friday on charges of insider trading, manipulating his company's inventory and securities fraud.

Emanuel Pinez, 58, an Israeli citizen who has homes in Canada, Switzerland and Beverly and Burlington, Mass., was until Tuesday the head of Centennial Technologies Inc., which saw it stock price increase 450 percent during the year to reach 58-1/4.

The exchange halted trading in the stock of the personal computer card maker Tuesday, shortly before the firm said it had fired Pinez. On Monday, its last day of trading, Centennial shares closed at 16-3/8.
Analysts expect the stock to open in the single digits, when and if, trading resumes.
FBI agents arrested Pinez at his Beverly, Mass., home early Friday after the Securities and Exchange Commission filed a complaint alleging he "shorted" his former company.

The federal complaint alleges that Pinez, bought and sold more than 4,400 option contracts at a time when he had orchestrated a number of accounting improprieties that were in the process of being investigated by the company's board of directors.

Beginning last Friday, Feb. 7, Pinez allegedly started buying put options and selling call options to expire on March 21, the complaint said. Call options give an investor the right to buy a stock at a certain price, will put option allow the sale at a certain price.
The SEC said Pinez's minimum profit on the call options will be $447,500.
"It's impossible to say right now how much his profit will be on the put options," SEC District Administrator Juan Marcel Marcelino said in a telephone interview.

Pinez also told the board at the Tuesday meeting where he was subsequently fired that he inflated the amount of inventory sold, the complaint said. He admitted advancing his personal money to customers to buy the inventory, the U.S. attorney said.
The complaint said Pinez borrowed more than $15 million "on margin" from two brokerage firms based on the market value of stock in his accounts.
If convicted, he faces up to five years in prison and $5,000 fine on each count of securities fraud as well as restitution. Investigators said the probe is continuing.
Pinez's lawyer, Robert Ullmann, former chief of the criminal division at the U.S. attorney's in Boston, said his client "vehemently denies any criminal wrong doing."
U.S. Magistrate Lawrence Cohen ordered Pinez detained, froze his assets and set a hearing date of Tuesday, Feb 18.
